QF.id: Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets_34

question.text: A puttable bond gives the right to:

answer.text: The issuer to call back the bond early
The bondholder to demand early repayment from the issuer
The regulator to cancel the bond
A third party to convert the bond to equity

explanation.text: The Logic: A puttable bond is an embedded-option bond in which the bondholder (not the issuer) holds the put — i.e., the right to demand early repayment of principal from the issuer, typically at par, on specified dates before the stated maturity. The feature protects the investor from deteriorating credit conditions or rising interest rates, because they can exit the bond and redeploy the proceeds. The Trap: An issuer's right to call the bond back early describes a callable bond, not a puttable bond. Regulators do not "cancel" the bond as a standard feature. Third-party conversion to equity describes convertible structures or exchangeables, not puttability. Note: The cited NISM Series XV Research Analyst workbook covers duration, inflation-protected securities, perpetual bonds with issuer callability and put options on equities, but the specific definition of a puttable bond (bondholder's right to demand early repayment) was not located on the pages checked. The framing above is general fixed-income/regulatory knowledge included for completeness.
